Canvas URI:   https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0170.JP2
Image API:    https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/image/b18775275_MS_990_0170.JP2/full/full/0/default.jpg (Dimensions: 5699 x 6853 px)
Red-Rule Box: https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0170.JP2#xywh=800,300,4599,6253 | Center Rule X=3099
Summary:      Folio 99 verso of Wellcome Collection MS.990 (c. 1675) continues a treatise on pestilential fever and its treatment. The left column outlines the fivefold (headed '4 weg') therapeutic regimen—air correction, vomitives, purgation via the bowels, sweating, and tempering of heat and cold—followed by diagnostic signs of acute thirst, precordial oppression, and shivering, and introduces a protective fumigation ('Rauch') accompanied by an illustration of a smoking censer. The right column provides the compound fumigation recipe (including olibanum, amber, myrrh, mastic, asa foetida, hartshorn, angelica, pimpernel, and spun hemp, silk, gold, and silver threads) and a section on therapeutic vomiting ('Yber brechen in disen fieber') illustrated by a man vomiting into a tub, recommending mild emetics such as linseed, walnut, or bitter almond oil, hazelwort with oxymel, and a feather dipped in scorpion oil.

Red-Rule Box: https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0171.JP2#xywh=300,300,4920,6253 | Center Rule X=2760
Summary:      Folio 208r of Wellcome MS.990 presents two columns of 17th-century German and Latin medical recipes and therapeutic instructions. The left column opens with a secret arcanum ('Ein schönes Arcana') prepared by distilling bryony root, cyclamen root, and white hellebore in water, administered in Malmsey wine via a small glass pipette (accompanied by an inline triangular symbol/sketch of the glass tip) to purge contagious poisons from the stomach, followed by a section attributed to 'H. Rönötten' on removing the cause of the illness through purgation, clysters, bloodletting, and especially sweating. The right column discusses sweating as a sure remedy for this and other fevers, warning against overheating ingredients (brandy, pepper, pellitory, castoreum, camphor, sulfur), debating whether camphor cools or heats, and providing several sudorific recipes (angelica root with theriac, elecampane in red wine, lovage root with wine vinegar, rue juice with theriac) as well as external warming methods using vinegar-moistened bricks, hot water flasks, and a vinegar-and-theriac compress applied over the navel.

Summary:      Page 201 (verso) in two columns. The upper left continues a regimen on managing sweat and preventing sleep in poisoned or feverish patients (including heart-strengthening cordials). The main section 'Vom Aderlasen' (Of Bloodletting) argues against bloodletting in this continuous fever because it weakens the body's moisture and drives heat toward the heart, brain, chest, or kidneys, followed by a red rubric noting that experience shows all who died had been bled. The right column concludes with remarks on aiding natural purgation (vomiting, suppositories, or laxative foods).

Summary:      Page 202 (recto) in two columns. Continues general remarks on fever heat, then presents 'Von der Hiz, und dero Küellung' (Of Heat and its Cooling), detailing cooling foods, waters, syrups (rose, violet, lemon, pomegranate, mulberry, elderberry, citron), and warning against applying cold poultices directly to the heart or stomach. The right column adds lukewarm ointments, cooling lotions (rosewater, nightshade, salt, rue), and introduces 'Von Allerley Zue fäll dises fiebers, als erstlich von der Tobsucht und haubt Wehe' (Of All Kinds of Symptoms of this Fever, Firstly Frenzy and Headache).

Summary:      Page 203 (verso), written in a single full-page column. Continues distinguishing the symptoms of hot/bilious headache and lethargy, then presents 'Von den hitzigen bösenden Kopff Wehe' (Of the Hot Malignant Headache) with recipes for rosewater, salt, Armenian bole, barley milk, and—if delirium ensues—applying a freshly split black hen or warm calf/lamb lung to the shaved head. Concludes with 'Von khalten Schläfferigen Wehe tage des Haubts' (Of Cold Lethargic Headache) and a spiced vinegar decoction (angelica, masterwort, zedoary, tormentil, dittany, red roses, marjoram, lavender).

Summary:      Page 205 (verso), arranged in two columns, continues the treatise on sweats ('Von den Schwaissen'), distinguishing two types: non-decretory cold/clammy sweats (with warnings against featherbeds, instructions to prevent sleep by applying red/rose vinegar with lavender or rosewater to the nose and pulses) and critical sweats ('sudores critici') on the 3rd, 5th, or 7th day (to be wiped with warm cloths and checked with quince or myrtle oil if excessive). In the lower right column, a major red-ink heading 'Von Vergicht, Krampf, Omachten und sewer gliedrn' introduces convulsions, cramps, fainting, and heavy limbs.

Summary:      Page 215, laid out in two columns, presents the treatment for fever pustules, petechiae, and smallpox-like eruptions. The left column warns against chilling the patient or overheating them with excessive bedclothes, and gives two detailed Latin apothecary recipes: a precious-stone cordial powder (bezoardic/cordial powder with pearls, corals, bole, ivory, dittany, camphor, zedoary, saffron, and behen) and a gilded electuary (conserve of roses, borage, bugloss, theriac, mithridate, gold leaf, and citron syrup). The right column offers topical and supportive remedies: lentil and fig waters with vinegar, white rose oil and Solomon's seal for facial skin, juniper-quince salves for ulcerating pustules, and woman's milk, rose honey, or pomegranate gargles for pustules in the mouth, eyes, nose, and throat.

No illustrations.

Begins a new major section 'Von Underschiedlichen Zuefälen So sich bey den hizigen fieber begeben' ('Of Various Symptoms Occurring in Hot Fevers'), starting with severe headache remedies. Summary:      Folio 227r is laid out in two columns. The left column continues the distilled pulmonary water recipe from f. 226v, adds a marshmallow-iris julep, warns against strong purgatives for consumptives (offering a mild laxative drink instead), and gives a laudanum/cynoglossum pill remedy for children's whooping cough. The right column concludes the pill recipe and presents a 'wonderful secretum' (aloes compress on the stomach), a 'precious lung drink' of herbs and raisins, 'Another' calf's-lung distillation, and a gold-leaf secretum for consumption.

Summary:      Folio 228v opens the chapter 'Von Bluet speiben' (On Spitting of Blood / Hemoptysis) in two columns. The upper-left features a colored watercolor illustration of a woman vomiting/spitting blood into a bowl. The left column explains the causes, diagnostic distinctions (lung vs. chest vs. stomach vs. head bleeding), and prognosis of hemoptysis. The right column discusses fever-related risks, bloodletting (arm, hand, foot, and leeches to the hemorrhoidal vein), dietary regimen, and three remedies: turpentine/Indian balsam pills with China/sarsaparilla decoction, a 'wonderful electuary' of henbane, poppy, terra sigillata, and red coral, and a 'special remedy' of crab ashes dissolved in vinegar.
Model:        Gemini 4 Hydrogen

Summary:      A 17th-century German and Latin medical manuscript page (folio 229r) containing remedies for haemorrhage and haemoptysis (spitting of blood). The left column presents several astringent powders, a secret remedy using eggshell membrane and plantain water, boluses, and a 'wonderful effect' recipe using mouse or rat dung. The right column continues with purgative/astringent instructions using rhubarb, oxymel, and theriac, followed by a decoction for spitting of blood, a chemical preparation of 'Balsam ♃' (balsam of sulphur/tin with turpentine), and a final section on treating haemoptysis with rhubarb, linden charcoal, and blessed thistle water.
Model:        Gemini 4 Hydrogen
Tokens Used:  Input: 1,350 | Output: 2,650

Summary:      Folio 230 verso from Wellcome Collection MS.990 (c. 1675), containing medical notes and recipes in Early New High German with Latin pharmaceutical terminology. The left column concludes a remedy for disordered blood (recommending rhubarb to draw water from the blood), followed by an ink-and-watercolor illustration of a patient inhaling medicinal vapors beneath a linen tent over a brazier. Below the illustration, a section titled 'Fluß Chatar' defines catarrh as phlegm and moisture rising from the stomach, spleen, liver, or womb into the head like vapors in an alembic, listing resulting ailments (apoplexy, abscesses, ear/eye/tooth pain, angina, suffocative catarrh, gout, sciatica). The right column continues the typology of cold and hot catarrhs, prescribes universal purges (emetics, Hauptpillen, syrups of betony, stoechas, calendula, sage, rosemary, violets, chicory), and provides two recipes in red-headed sections: a fumigation ('Volgenter Rauch Ist Köstlich') with white amber, mastic, cloves, and masterwort, and a medicated head fomentation/cap ('Bäthe auf das haubt für Catar... f. Scuffia') with hartshorn, barley, bran, marjoram, betony, red roses, Arabian stoechas, camel's hay, fennel, sweet flag, and mastic.

Red-Rule Box: https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0201.JP2#xywh=300,300,4871,6253 | Center Rule X=2735
Summary:      Folio 231 recto from Wellcome MS.990 (c. 1675) presents German and Latin medical recipes and clinical commentary in two columns. The left column contains four fumigation (Rauch) recipes for hot and cold catarrhs and fluxes of the head, followed by an electuary and mutton-broth remedy for prolonged coughing and wheezing, and begins a section on hot catarrh (Von den Hitzigen Catarrn). The right column continues the treatment of hot catarrh—discussing bloodletting, a rhubarb-tamarind purgative, laudanum opiatum, and chest syrups (including coltsfoot), as well as hoarseness—before introducing a new major section on coughing (Von dem Huesten), detailing its physiology, causes (phlegm from the head, vapors from liver, stomach, spleen, or womb, and lung ulcers), and therapeutic cautions.

[c0203_left_l04]       (#xywh=300,683,2417,127)   leiden ligt. oder der kranckheit schwierig
[c0203_left_l05]       (#xywh=300,810,2417,128)   überwunden. so der kranckh aber bei diser

[c0203_left_l07]       (#xywh=300,1066,2417,127)  kranckh[eit] ist dise. das bei der hend

[c0204_right_2_l05]    (#xywh=3136,3079,2297,695) auch khom[men] Von Zu uillen drei schner(?) oder feichte. es khumbt
[c0204_right_2_l06]    (#xywh=3136,3774,2297,695) auch mehren thail Von einer intemperirt[en] Leber. dan
[c0204_right_2_l07]    (#xywh=3136,4469,2297,694) selbige khan guettes bluett macht, Welliches dem herzen
[c0204_right_2_l08]    (#xywh=3136,5163,2297,695) zu hilft. so hat das herz darvon kheine guete Nahrung. oder aber
[c0204_right_2_l09]    (#xywh=3136,5858,2297,695) das blutt ist zu will oder hizig. oder gar zu dickh. es khumbt

Summary:      Folio 236v (two columns) continues the prognosis and treatment of breast aposteme/empyema. The left column provides emollient poultices and plasters, a pectoral decoction ('Prust Tranckh'), and a linctus ('Zum Leckhen Dis Xolgendes'). The right column describes surgical thoracentesis (incising between the third and fourth ribs to drain pus gradually), a supplementary linseed/sugar remedy, and concludes with a section on 'Prust Wassersucht' (hydrothorax / dropsy of the breast).

Summary:      Folio 237r (two columns) features a large hand-colored sickbed illustration at the top of the left column, followed by a treatise 'Von den Schmerzlichen Seiden Stechen' (Of the Painful Side-Stitches / Pleurisy). The text defines true pleurisy (pleuritis exquisita / legitima) as an inflammation of the pleura and lists its five cardinal symptoms. The right column continues the symptoms, prognostic signs (including conversion to empyema after 14 days and the critical 7th day), and introduces false pleurisy ('Das falsche Seiden stich Spuria oder Bastärdt').

At the top of the left column is a red-wash anatomical illustration of the stomach above an empty cartouche. The text discusses the humoral causes of stomach ailments (viscous phlegm, bile, melancholy, heat, and cold), the physiological role of the pylorus and stomach ferment in digestion, relaxation of the pylorus leading to lientery/diarrhea, remedies including hard egg yolks, nutmeg, and a closing powder, and symptoms of bilious heat versus cold phlegmatic matter in the stomach.

Summary:      Page 240 (recto) continues the discussion of stomach ailments, addressing cold phlegmatic accumulation, sympathetic illness from the liver, dietary excesses, and the difficulty of curing chronic cold stomach conditions. It recommends emetics (blessed water, English salt, Tartarum Emeticum) followed by a herbal decoction of mint, betony, calamus, angelica, and mastic. The second half of the page discusses the causes of stomach weakness ('Die Schwachheit des Magen khumbt Von'), particularly overeating and excessive purging.

Summary:      Page 241 (verso) presents treatments for weakness of the stomach ('Cur in Schwacheit des Magn'), beginning with internal preparatory syrups (syrup of violets and roses with lentisk or tamarind), purgative pills of rhubarb and aloes, and a cooling decoction for the hot liver. It then gives multiple external recipes: fomentations ('Fumonda') with aromatic herbs in red wine or sour water, strengthening plasters with labdanum, aloes, and expressed nutmeg oil, three variations of herbal stomach bags ('Magn Säckhel'), and a warming stomach ointment ('Salbe') for a cold, weak stomach.
Model:        Gemini 4 Hydrogen
Tokens Used:  Input: 2,800 | Output: 2,600

The right column continues with dietary and seasonal rules for bloodletting (wine vs. food, May/April vs. autumn, purging before venesection) and warnings against bleeding young children, pregnant or menstruating women, and postpartum patients.

Summary:      Page 260 (recto) features a full-length red-ink anatomical illustration of the arterial system (numbered 114) in the left column, captioned 'Vena Pulsatilis Arteria', with text explaining that the artery originates in the left chamber of the heart and carries the most subtle vital spirits. The right column discusses the danger of accidentally striking an artery during bloodletting (especially near the liver vein), quantifies the pulse rate in healthy men (4,000 beats/hour) and choleric women (4,800 beats/hour), and introduces the section 'Von Greiffung der Puls' (On Feeling the Pulse), distinguishing pulse quantity (length, breadth, depth) and quality.

Red-Rule Box: https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0234.JP2#xywh=800,300,4654,6253 | Center Rule X=3127
Summary:      Page 261 (verso) continues the treatise on pulse diagnostics, cataloging the qualitative varieties of the pulse according to classical Galenic sphygmology: equal and unequal pulses, the recurrent pulse in the elderly, the intermittent/sawing ('verchlofne') pulse, the undulating wave-like ('wellende') pulse, the goat-leaping ('Caprisissa'), worm-like ('Wurmechtige / Vermicansa'), ant-like ('ameissige / formicansa') pulses—warning that the latter three portend death—as well as the trembling ('ziterte') pulse, the intercidens pulse in young healthy subjects, and weak pulses in malignant fevers.
Model:        Gemini 4 Hydrogen
Tokens Used:  Input: 1,290 | Output: 1,950

Summary:      Folio 262r continues a medical treatise on sphygmology (pulse diagnosis). It discusses the difficulty of recognizing the pulse, the proper comportment and technique of the physician when approaching the patient and taking the pulse (arm position, four-finger palpation, delicacy of hand, patient stillness and fasting, taking both hands, considering the patient's complexion and body heat), and variations of the pulse according to sex and age (men vs. women, elderly, youths, and children), concluding with an aphorism on the supreme importance of pulse knowledge.
Model:        Gemini 4 Hydrogen

Summary:      Folio 284r continues the treatise on the soul, defining it as a heavenly, undivided essence and the true form of man that operates through the body's limbs. The right column enumerates its Latin designations (ratio, Mens, Animus, Sensus et intellectus) and classifies the four principal faculties of the soul: sensibility (empfindtligkheit), imagination (einbildung), judgment (Urtheill), and memory (gedächtnuß), beginning with an exposition of internal sensation.

Summary:      Folio 285v continues the account of the internal senses, explaining how the five external senses converge into the common sense like lines to the center of a circle, and locating judgment in the third cell of the brain. It then treats fantasy/imagination (active even in sleep and dreams, and capable of moving the body in anger or joy) and, below a portrait bust of a curly-haired youth, introduces reason/judgment as the highest faculty of the soul.

Summary:      Recto folio 127 (page 286). Left column concludes a discussion of anger/passions and proceeds to a section on memory ('Nach der Vernunfft Volgt die gedechtnuß'), locating it in the cerebellum or fourth cell of the brain. Right column begins a major section on the division of the human body and its faculties ('Von abtheilung des menschen Leibs, Und Von der glider underscheidt'), classifying them into Animal (Seeliche), Vital (Leibliche), and Natural (Natürliche) powers.

Summary:      Recto folio 128 (page 288). Left column discusses the proper and improper use of the six non-natural things (citing Galen) and begins a major section on sleep ('Von den Schlaffen'). Right column treats the benefits of timely sleep, the harmfulness of midday sleep ('Der mittagige Schlaff ist Sehr schädlich'), optimal sleep duration (7–8 hours), diagnostic signs in urine and stomach after sleep, and begins a rubric on excessive waking.

Summary:      Recto folio 292 opening the chapter on 'Melancolia. hipocontrica.' (Hypochondriac Melancholy). The upper left features a coloured ink-and-wash portrait of a melancholic man holding a staff and a celestial globe on a golden stand beside a four-paned window showing a starry night sky and crescent moon. The text describes the humoral etiology (burnt blood collecting in the mesenteric veins, affecting spleen, stomach, heart, and brain), physical symptoms (bloating, constipation, palpitations, dizziness, cold sweat), and behavioral manifestations (solitude, avoidance of company, devotion to reading and study).

Summary:      Verso folio 293, written in a single full-width column, continuing the treatise on hypochondriac melancholy. It discusses excessive sleep, heaviness of limbs, vertigo, tinnitus, diagnostic signs distinguishing spleen, liver, and stomach involvement, therapeutic principles (balancing a cold stomach with a hot liver, purgation, diet, and sweat-cures), and opens a new rubricated section on the effects of melancholia hypochondriaca.

Summary:      Recto folio 294, arranged in two columns, continuing the account of the effects of melancholia hypochondriaca. It details the patient's changeable appetite, strange delusions, hemorrhoids ('guldine ader'), progression to chronic illness with quartan fever, and the physician's predicament—receiving blame, ingratitude, and slander from obstinate patients who constantly complain and change doctors. It concludes by identifying the primary cause as sour, foul moisture in the stomach from poor digestion, exacerbated by salted/spiced meats, sedentary habits, and excessive nocturnal study.

Summary:      Page 295 (recto) discusses the pathophysiology of hypochondriacal melancholy, attributing it to unnatural fermentation in the intestines and acidity in the blood, and warns against bloodletting and overly harsh purges. It prescribes mild preparatory remedies (such as tincture of tartar and spirit of salt) and lists beneficial herbs and minerals. The right column features a watercolor illustration of four apothecary or drinking vessels on a shelf, followed by recipes for a decoction and a purgative draught for melancholy.

Summary:      Page 298 (recto) of Wellcome MS.990 contains early modern German and Latin medical recipes arranged in two columns, focusing on remedies for hypochondria, melancholy, flatulence, constipation, and blood purification. Treatments include borage flower infusions, rhubarb lozenges (Zeltl), a distilled spirit, blood-purifying herbal infusions, cheese-water (whey) infusions, a Maschanzker apple syrup with kermes or crimson silk for melancholy and heart palpitations, and purging little balls (Purgier Bälßel) to expel black bile and melancholic humors.

Summary:      Page 299 (verso) of Wellcome MS.990 presents sudorific (sweating) remedies and laxative decoctions for purifying the blood and treating melancholy. The left column lists diaphoretic antimony and hartshorn powders, followed by a laxative draught of goat's milk whey, senna, and rhubarb, and a 20-day sarsaparilla and china-root decoction. The right column provides two complex herbal decoctions for stirring the spleen, liver, and mesenteric veins and evacuating burnt bile and phlegm, concluding with a gentle purging decoction of prunes, sebestens, jujubes, tamarinds, cassia, and manna.

Summary:      Page 300 (recto) of Wellcome MS.990 opens in the left column with a small painted illustration of three red-filled bowls on a rectangular shelf beside the heading 'Absiesung des gebliedts' (Sweetening/tempering of the blood). The left column lists absorbent and blood-thinning remedies (crabs' eyes, corals, hartshorn, spirit of scurvy-grass, tincture of steel, and acidity-tempering herbs). The right column contains faded red rubrics for powders and pills with camphor and Peruvian balsam, a blood-purifying compound for severe conditions including leprosy and the Neapolitan disease (syphilis), and a concluding 'wonderful blood-purifying and expelling remedy' prepared as an electuary.

Summary:      Page 303 (recto) transitions from melancholy and blood purification to diseases of the spleen. The left column features an anatomical watercolor illustration of a spleen with its branching vessels, followed by a discussion of the shared remedies and physiological relationship between the liver and spleen, the obstruction of the portal vein, and the spleen's office of drawing melancholic humor. The right column describes symptoms of splenic illness (flatulence, vertigo, tinnitus, diaphragm oppression, chills, quartan fevers, inflammation) and their causes (over-eating, cold slimy food, drinking in heat, studying after meals).

The right column outlines the therapeutic regimen: beginning with purgatives (rhubarb, aloes, agaric), followed by resolving steel/tartar powders, emetics if the stomach is slimy, and specific pill formulations (including Dr. Bontius's pills), steel-infused wine, and an aromatic confection.

Summary:      Continuation of the treatise on arthritis/gout: distinguishing Podagra from true arthritis; the causes of the disease ('Die Vrsach diser khranckheit sind Vnderschidlich'), including overeating/overdrinking, anger, strong wine, sharp brain fluxes, heavy lifting, and chilling; prognosis (generally not fatal and often associated with longevity, though dangerous in weak old age, potentially leading to fever, pleurisy, stroke, or palpitations); and treatment via diet, abstention from wine and sour foods, purging/evacuation, and prescribed pills followed by mineral salt and oil.

Summary:      Early New High German medical and apothecary recipes (verso, p. 503) in two columns. The left column continues treatments for burns and gangrene (using frog spawn, green willow bark in butter, egg white with prepared tutty, rose oil, linseed oil, unslaked lime, and litharge). The right column contains three rubricated recipes in red ink for frostbitten hands and feet in winter, swelling of the feet, and a precious medicinal water (with mercury sublimate) for rising, swelling, ulcers, and scabby eruptions of the feet and hands.
Model:        Gemini 4 Hydrogen
Tokens Used:  Input: 1,850 | Output: 2,350

Summary:      Surgical treatise 'Von fistlen in Gemain' (Of fistulas in general), accompanied by a watercolor illustration of a seated man with red lesions/fistulas on his face, arms, and legs. The text discusses probing fistulas to assess depth and hidden passages, widening openings with tent dilators (Stellmeißel), deciding between surgical excision/cauterization and palliative care near major nerves and blood vessels, and supporting local treatment with strict diet, purgatives, decoctions, and wound potions.

Summary:      Early New High German medical/apothecary manuscript (Wellcome MS.990, p. 565, verso). The left column concludes a treatment note and presents a rubricated section on the signs and diagnosis of fistulas (distinguishing marrow, nerve/membrane, flesh, blood-vessel, and carious-bone fistulas, followed by dietary and caustic treatment advice). The right column begins a rubricated section on fistulas of the breast/chest, followed by four Latin-German apothecary recipes: a precious plaster for fistulas with preparation instructions, two salves/liniments, and a caustic wash for spongy flesh in fistulas.

Summary:      Continuation of a medical treatise on syphilis (Franzosenkrankheit / Morbus Gallicus), detailing its symptoms (pustules, bone pains, ulceration of the uvula, tonsils, throat, and genitals, dark circles under the eyes, general weakness, and latency periods) and five methods of treatment: (1) the wood cure (guaiac, sassafras, sarsaparilla, China root), (2) purgation with mercurials (mercurius dulcis, arcanum corallinum, white precipitate, turpethum minerale), (3) the fumigation/smoke cure with cinnabar, (4) the inunction/ointment cure with mercury, and (5) bathing in mercurial sublimate water. The author concludes that among these five cures, the mercury inunction cure is the best and most reliable.

Image API:    https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/image/b18775275_MS_990_0671.JP2/full/full/0/default.jpg (Dimensions: 2400 x 3111 px)
Red-Rule Box: https://iiif.wellcomecollection.org/presentation/b18775275/canvases/b18775275_MS_990_0671.JP2#xywh=300,300,1300,2511 | Center Rule X=950
Summary:      Surgical and medical treatise on abdominal and urological wounds in 17th-century German. The left column continues instructions for suturing and treating wounds of the small and large intestines, including using a cannula/tube (Röhrl), applying a hemostatic powder (℞ mastic, frankincense, aloes, mumia, dragon's blood), and fomenting prolapsed, bloated intestines with warm wine. The right column concludes intestinal wound care (including references to iliac passion and sarsaparilla), then presents two rubricated sections accompanied by watercolor anatomical illustrations: 'Das Kress mesenterij' (wounds of the mesentery, with a crescent-shaped illustration) and 'Die Wunden der Niern vnnd Plasen' (wounds of the kidneys and bladder, with illustrations of two kidneys with renal vessels/ureters and a bladder), detailing diagnostic signs (bloody urine, urine leaking from the wound) and a kidney wound balm recipe.
Model:        Gemini 4 Hydrogen

Summary:      Page 48 recto contains an anatomical treatise and watercolor flap diagram (Klappbild) of the human eye ('Anatomia oder Zerlegung des Augs'), shown here with the outer anatomical flap closed (displaying the sclera/conjunctiva F and iris/pupil H). Column 1 presents the watercolor eye diagrams, muscle/tunic key, and a rubricated list of the seven eye membranes; Column 2 provides the rubricated title, anatomical key A–R, and prose explanations of the origins of the eye's membranes.
